# Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH {#sec-p2}

## Summary

**Modelling the volatility of the rand with GARCH models** (Part 1, ARCH / GARCH; implementation project; covers real-world data and model comparison).

This project asks whether the USD/ZAR exchange rate shows volatility clustering, which GARCH-type model and error distribution describe it best, and how persistent shocks to the rand's volatility are. I used daily USD/ZAR closing rates from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2025, downloaded from Yahoo Finance with `quantmod::getSymbols("ZAR=X")` and converted to daily log returns in percent, $r_t = 100 \times \log(P_t / P_{t-1})$, after removing days with missing values and six extreme outlier returns. After exploring the returns and squared returns (ACF, ARCH LM test), I chose a constant mean using the Ljung-Box test and an ARMA comparison. I then fitted GARCH(1,1) models with `rugarch` using normal, Student t and skewed t errors, added GJR-GARCH and EGARCH, and compared them with QQ plots, AIC/BIC and standardised residual diagnostics.

The returns are uncorrelated but show strong volatility clustering (ARCH LM test $p < 0.001$). The best model was a constant mean with GJR-GARCH(1,1) and skewed t errors ($\hat\xi = 1.18$, $\hat\nu = 14.7$), which beat the normal and Student t errors and the symmetric GARCH on AIC and BIC. Volatility rises mostly after positive returns (rand weakening), since $\hat\delta = -0.037$ almost cancels $\hat\alpha_1 = 0.042$ for negative shocks, and persistence is very high ($\hat\rho = 0.9956$, half-life about 158 days). The predicted price is essentially the previous day's price, so the model's value is the changing width of the prediction band rather than the point forecast.

If I did this again, I would address three limitations. The residual tests still show weak short-lag dependence in the squared residuals, and GJR(2,1) and (1,2) did not remove it, so I would try other variance structures. The long-run volatility is poorly estimated (0.72% against a sample standard deviation of 0.96%), because persistence is near one and $\hat\alpha_0$ is not significant. I would also refit before and after 2020 to check for a structural break, and evaluate the forecasts out of sample. A full detailed analysis follows below.

## Data and EDA

### Downloading the data

This project used ARCH and GARCH models to analyse the volatility of daily USD/ZAR exchange rate data from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2025. The data was downloaded from Yahoo Finance using the `quantmod` package, and days with missing values were removed from the data set. Each observation is the daily closing USD/ZAR exchange rate (rand per US dollar), which is the rate at the end of that day’s trading.

```{r}
#| output: false
library(quantmod)
library(rugarch)
library(FinTS)
library(here)
library(tidyverse)

file_path <- here("data", "usdzar.csv")

if (!file.exists(file_path)) {
  zar <- getSymbols("ZAR=X", src = "yahoo", from = "2015-01-01", to = "2025-12-31",
                    auto.assign = FALSE)
  zar <- Cl(zar)
  write.csv(data.frame(date = index(zar), exchange_rate = as.numeric(zar)), file_path, row.names = FALSE)
}

data <- read.csv(file_path)
sapply(data, class)
data$date <- as.Date(data$date)
nrow(data)
range(data$date)
sum(is.na(data))
data <- na.omit(data)
nrow(data)
range(data$date)
sum(is.na(data))
```

### EDA and outliers

Our first step is to analyse the data visually. @fig-price_level below plots the exchange rate (or the price level) at close for each day over the time period of interest.

```{r}
#| label: fig-price_level
#| fig-cap: "Daily USD/ZAR exchange rates"

plot(data$date, data$exchange_rate, type = "l", xlab = "time", ylab = "rands per dollar (price level)")
```

The upward trend over time in @fig-price_level above shows that over the 11 years from the start of 2015 to the end of 2025, the exchange rate increased. One dollar only was worth roughly R12, but at the end one dollar was worth nearly R18. The value of the Rand has an inverse relationship with the USD/ZAR exchange rate, and thus the value of the Rand relative to the dollar decreased over this period as the price level increased. As there is a clear trend, the data is not stationary. We can confirm this with a Ljung-Box test for autocorrelation.

```{r}
Box.test(data$exchange_rate, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")
```

The p-value < 0.001 shows there is significant evidence of autocorrelation.

When working with financial data, we are usually more interested in returns $r_t$ than price levels $P_t$. There are three types of returns. Simple return shows the percentage change in the price. Gross returns are ratio amount by which the price level increased or decreased from one day to the next. Logarithmic returns show the log of the gross returns and are most preferable as you can add log returns over time to get the total return for that period. @fig-returns below shows simple and log returns for our data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-returns
#| fig-cap: "Daily simple returns in percent (top) and logarithmic returns in percent (bottom), before cleaning."
#| fig-height: 8

data$simple_return      <- c(NA, 100 * diff(data$exchange_rate) / head(data$exchange_rate, -1))
data$gross_return       <- 1 + data$simple_return / 100
data$logarithmic_return <- 100 * log(data$gross_return)
returns <- data$logarithmic_return[-1] # first value is always NA

par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(data$date, data$simple_return, type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "R_t",
     main = "Simple returns")
plot(data$date, data$logarithmic_return, type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "r_t",
     main = "Logarithmic returns")
```

In @fig-returns above, we see that differencing has removed the upward trend that was present on the price level data. However, there are several returns around November 2024 and January 2025 that are drastically different from the others. If we look at how the return data is distributed, we see that the data looks normally distributed around 0, with some outliers reaching positive and minus 20. This is evident in @fig-outliers below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-outliers
#| fig-cap: "Density (left) and boxplot (right) of the daily logarithmic returns before cleaning."

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(density(returns), main = "Density of returns")
boxplot(returns, main = "Boxplot of returns", ylab = "r_t")

summary(returns)
```

In @fig-outliers, the density plot shows that there are very long tails, and the boxplot shows that the outliers are much bigger in absolute value than most of the data. These outliers are evident in the normal quantile plot in @fig-qq below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq
#| fig-cap: "Normal QQ plot of the logarithmic returns before cleaning."
qqnorm(returns, main = "Normal QQ plot of returns"); qqline(returns, col = "red")
```

@fig-qq above shows that most of the returns appear normal, but the values in the tails are outliers. All the outliers have an absolute value greater than 12, with the next highest being less than 5. @tbl-outliers shows these returns, together with the price on the day before and the day after each one, and @fig-outlier-plot marks them in red on the original price level and return series.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-outliers
#| tbl-cap: "Returns with an absolute value above 5%, with the price on the days before and after."
data |>
  mutate(prev_price = lag(exchange_rate), next_price = lead(exchange_rate)) |>
  filter(abs(logarithmic_return) > 5) |>
  select(date, prev_price, exchange_rate, next_price, logarithmic_return) |>
  mutate(across(-date, ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-outlier-plot
#| fig-cap: "Daily USD/ZAR price (top) and logarithmic returns (bottom) before cleaning, with the outliers shown in red."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
outliers <- data |> filter(abs(logarithmic_return) > 5)

par(mfrow = c(2, 1))

plot(data$date, data$exchange_rate, type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "rands per dollar",
     main = "Price level")
points(outliers$date, outliers$exchange_rate, col = "red", pch = 16)

plot(data$date, data$logarithmic_return, type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "r_t",
     main = "Logarithmic returns")
points(outliers$date, outliers$logarithmic_return, col = "red", pch = 16)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

In @fig-outlier-plot, the six outliers come from three single days (15 November 2024, 15 January 2025 and 17 January 2025) where the price drops to between R14.9 and R16.5, while the prices around those days are between R18.2 and R19.0. Each of these produces two outlier returns, the fall and the rebound the following day, which is visible in @tbl-outliers. Because the price reverts straight back, these look like data errors rather than genuine movements in the rand, so we remove them.

After identifying the outliers, we remove them from the data, and repeat our plots of the data as we did previously to see how things now look. Each of these plots are shown in @fig-returns_clean below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-returns_clean
#| fig-cap: "Repeat of plots to check for outliers"
#| fig-height: 8

data_clean <- data |> 
  filter(abs(logarithmic_return) <= 5)

returns <- data_clean$logarithmic_return[-1] # first value is always NA


data_clean$simple_return <- c(NA, 100 * diff(data_clean$exchange_rate) / head(data_clean$exchange_rate, -1))
data_clean$gross_return <- 1 + data_clean$simple_return / 100
data_clean$logarithmic_return <- 100 * log(data_clean$gross_return)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

plot(data_clean$date, data_clean$logarithmic_return, type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "r_t",
     main = "Logarithmic returns")
plot(density(data_clean$logarithmic_return[-1]), main = "Density of returns")
boxplot(data_clean$logarithmic_return[-1], main = "Boxplot of returns", ylab = "r_t")
qqnorm(data_clean$logarithmic_return[-1], main = "Normal QQ plot of returns"); qqline(returns, col = "red")
```

We can clearly see from each of the plots in @fig-returns_clean above that there are no further clear outliers, and we are ready to begin our analysis. 

### ACF of returns and squared returns

Next, we check for evidence of volatility clustering in the logarithmic return data (from now on referred to as "returns"). We do this by using ACF plots of the returns, as shown in @fig-acf below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-acf
#| fig-cap: "ACF plot of logarithmic returns (left) and squared logarithmic returns (right)"

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(returns, main = "returns")
acf(returns^2, main = "squared returns")
```

In addition to the above @fig-acf, we also perform an ARCH LM test to check if the squared residuals have significant autocorrelation. 

```{r}
ArchTest(returns, lags = 12)
```

The ARCH test checks for conditional heteroscedasticity in the data. The ACF returns plot shows there is little or no significant correlation at any lags. The couple significant spikes are expected due to random chance when checking over 30 lags. However, the ACF on the squared residuals shows that there are many significant lags. In addition, the ARCH LM test show that there is significant autocorrelation among squared residuals within the first 12 lags. These findings are both evidence that there is volatility clustering in the data, and that the magnitude of a shock is not independent of the magnitude of previous shocks.

## ARCH / GARCH Models

ARCH / GARCH models have two components, where the returns $r_t$ are a combination of a mean equation $\mu_t$ and a variance equation $\varepsilon_t$, which gives us,

$$r_t = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t.$$

The aim of our model is to choose mean and variance equations that best explain our data $r_t$.

### Mean Equation

First we have our mean equation $\mu_t$. We have two options for our mean equation, either we can use a constant mean,

$$\mu_t = \mu,$$

or we can model the mean using an ARMA(p, q) model,

$$\mu_t = \mu + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \phi_i r_{t-i} + \sum_{j=1}^{q} \theta_j \varepsilon_{t-j}$$

We use a Ljung-Box test to check for autocorrelation in the log returns.

```{r}
Box.test(returns, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")
```

The Ljung-Box test has a p-value of 0.4588. There is not enough evidence to suggest that there is autocorrelation in the data, even at a 0.1 significance level. Thus, a constant mean is adequate for the returns.

We can investigate further by fitting multiple ARMA models to the data to confirm if a constant mean, an ARMA(0,0), is the best choice. We compare ARMA(0,0), ARMA(1,0), ARMA(0,1), and ARMA(1,1) in @tbl-arma below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-arma
#| tbl-cap: "Log-likelihood, AIC and BIC for four ARMA models for the mean of the returns."
ARMA_00 <- arima(returns, order = c(0,0,0), include.mean = TRUE)
ARMA_10 <- arima(returns, order = c(1,0,0), include.mean = TRUE)
ARMA_01 <- arima(returns, order = c(0,0,1), include.mean = TRUE)
ARMA_11 <- arima(returns, order = c(1,0,1), include.mean = TRUE)

data.frame(
  Model      = c("ARMA(0,0)", "ARMA(1,0)", "ARMA(0,1)", "ARMA(1,1)"),
  Parameters = c(2, 3, 3, 4),
  LogLik     = round(c(logLik(ARMA_00), logLik(ARMA_10), logLik(ARMA_01), logLik(ARMA_11)), 2),
  AIC        = round(c(AIC(ARMA_00), AIC(ARMA_10), AIC(ARMA_01), AIC(ARMA_11)), 2),
  BIC        = round(c(BIC(ARMA_00), BIC(ARMA_10), BIC(ARMA_01), BIC(ARMA_11)), 2))
```

From @tbl-arma above we see that there is little difference in log-likelihood between the models, and that the gains from adding more model parameters is minimal. In addition, both AIC and BIC scores increase as model complexity increases, indicating the increase performance is due to fitting the noise in the data. Based on this comparison, best form for the mean equation is a constant mean.

However, the ARIMA model assumes constant variance, which is not an assumption made in GARCH models. The coefficient for $\mu$ from the ARMA(0,0) will not equal the $\mu$ found by a GARCH model that assumes a constant mean. As our ARMA models suggest a constant mean, and our Ljung-Box test showed there was no significant autocorrelation in the data, for our model, we will use a constant mean in our mean equation. This gives us the following,

$$\mu_t = \mu, \qquad \text{and}$$

$$r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t.$$

### Variance Equation

Next we have our variance (or shock) equation,

$$\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} (0, 1)$$

In the above variance equation, we have $z_t$ the random white noise error term, and we have our conditional variance term $\sigma_t$ which we derive as follows,

$$\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j \sigma_{t-j}^2.$$

Like the mean equation, we want to choose a variance equation that describes how the conditional variance of $r_t$ changes over time, so that the uncertainty around our predictions of $r_t$ is more realistic. If the variance was not conditional over time, we would have,

$$
\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 = 1, \qquad \text{making} \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t =z_t.
$$

As our above ARCH LM-test and ACF plot of squared residuals both suggest there is conditional variance, we will use a GARCH model. In most cases, a GARCH(1,1) is most suitable, so we will start with that form in our modeling. This, in addition to our constant mean model, gives us the following for $r_t = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t$,

$$\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2$$

$$\therefore \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t = \sqrt{\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2}\; z_t$$

$$\therefore \qquad  r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t = \mu + \sqrt{\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2}\; z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} D(0, 1).$$

In addition to estimating parameters for the variance equation $\alpha_0$, $\alpha_1$ and $\beta_1$, we also have to choose a distribution $D$ for the error term $z_t$, which can be modelled using either a normal distribution, or a student-t distribution. Determining which form of variance equation to use will be done during modeling below.

## rugarch Models

Having chosen a constant mean, we use the `rugarch` package to fit a GARCH(1,1) variance equation. We use GARCH(1,1) as it is the standard specification and higher orders add extra parameters without improving model performance. The general GARCH(p, q) model with a constant mean has the parameters,

$$\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_q,\ \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p),$$

which for GARCH(1,1) gives us, 

$$r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} D(0,1),$$

$$\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,$$

$$\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1).$$

We estimate the $\theta$ parameters using maximum likelihood.

### Normally Distributed Errors

We first fit the model with normal errors, $z_t \sim N(0, 1)$, and use a quantile plot of the standardised residuals to check whether a heavier-tailed distribution is needed. This is shown in @fig-qq-norm below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq-norm
#| fig-cap: "QQ plot of the standardised residuals of the GARCH(1,1) model with normal errors."

make_spec <- function(model, dist) {
  ugarchspec(variance.model = list(model = model, garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
             mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
             distribution.model = dist)
}

fit_n <- ugarchfit(make_spec("sGARCH", "norm"), data = returns)
round(fit_n@fit$robust.matcoef, 4)

z_n <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_n, standardize = TRUE))

qqnorm(z_n, main = "QQ plot of standardised residuals (normal GARCH)")
qqline(z_n, col = "red")
```

The QQ plot in @fig-qq-norm shows that most of the standardised residuals follow what we would expect under normality, but the right tail is heavier than the normal distribution would predict. 

### Student-t Errors

We therefore refit with Student t errors, which adds the degrees of freedom $\nu$ (smaller $\nu$ means heavier tails), giving us the follow,

$$r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} t_\nu,$$

$$\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,$$

$$\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \nu).$$

The QQ plot using Student t distributed residuals is shown in @fig-qqt below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-qqt
#| fig-cap: "QQ plot of the standardised residuals against the fitted Student t distribution."
fit_t <- ugarchfit(make_spec("sGARCH", "std"), data = returns)
round(fit_t@fit$robust.matcoef, 4)

# QQ plot of the standardised residuals against the fitted t distribution
z_t <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_t, standardize = TRUE))
nu  <- coef(fit_t)["shape"]
n   <- length(z_t)

qqplot(qt(ppoints(n), nu) * sqrt((nu - 2) / nu), z_t,
       xlab = "Theoretical t quantiles", ylab = "Standardised residuals",
       main = "QQ plot against fitted t (GARCH-t)")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
```

In @fig-qqt above, the QQ plot of the Student t model shows an improvement, as the right tail is now closer to the red line. However, the left tail is now lighter than the fitted t expects, while the right tail is still slightly heavier. This suggests that the tails are asymmetric.

### Skew Student-t Errors

The Student t is symmetric, so it cannot fit both tails at once. To address this, we will fit a model using a skew Student-t distribution, which adds a skewness parameter $\xi$, which gives the following,

$$r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{skew-}t_{\xi,\nu},$$

$$\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,$$

$$\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \xi,\ \nu).$$

We again use a QQ plot to assess the model fit, as shown in @fig-qqst below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-qqst
#| fig-cap: "QQ plot of the standardised residuals against the fitted skewed t distribution."
fit_st <- ugarchfit(make_spec("sGARCH", "sstd"), data = returns)
round(fit_st@fit$robust.matcoef, 4)

# QQ plot of the standardised residuals against the fitted skewed t distribution
z_st <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_st, standardize = TRUE))
q_st <- qdist("sstd", p = ppoints(length(z_st)), mu = 0, sigma = 1,
              skew = coef(fit_st)["skew"], shape = coef(fit_st)["shape"])

qqplot(q_st, z_st,
       xlab = "Theoretical skewed t quantiles", ylab = "Standardised residuals",
       main = "QQ plot against fitted skewed t (GARCH-skewed t)")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
```

### Model Comparison

The three models share the same mean and variance equations, they only differ in the distribution of $z_t$. The normal has no extra parameters, the Student t adds $\nu$, and the skewed t adds $\xi$ as well. We compare the AIC and BIC scores of the three models in @tbl-errordist below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-errordist
#| tbl-cap: "AIC and BIC (per observation) for the three error distributions."
ic <- cbind( # comparing the normal, t and skewed t fits
  GARCH_normal = infocriteria(fit_n)[1:2, 1],
  GARCH_t      = infocriteria(fit_t)[1:2, 1],
  GARCH_sstd   = infocriteria(fit_st)[1:2, 1]
)
round(ic, 4) |> as.data.frame()
```

For both AIC and BIC in @tbl-errordist above, the GARCH model using skew Student t errors outperforms the models with normal errors and the student t errors. Given the QQ plot on the skew Student t model was also the best, we will use skew Student t errors in our model, which gives us the following final model,

$$r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \text{with errors},$$

$$\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{skew-}t_{\xi,\nu} \text{ (0, 1)}, \qquad \text{where},$$

$$\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2, \qquad \text{and parameters},$$

$$\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \xi,\ \nu).$$

### GJR-GARCH and EGARCH

The GARCH(1,1) variance equation depends on $\varepsilon_{t-1}^2$, so it responds identically to positive and negative shocks of the same size (§7.11). The skewed t errors allow the two tails of $z_t$ to differ, but they do not change this. To allow the variance to respond asymmetrically (the leverage effect), we fit two asymmetric GARCH models, GJR-GARCH and EGARCH, keeping skewed t errors. Both have the same mean equation and error distribution,

$$r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{skew-}t_{\xi,\nu},$$

and differ in the variance equation. The GJR-GARCH adds a term that is switched on only for negative shocks,

$$\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \left(\alpha_1 + \delta\,\mathbb{1}[\varepsilon_{t-1}<0]\right)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,$$

$$\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \delta,\ \xi,\ \nu),$$

while the EGARCH models the log of the variance, so no positivity restrictions are needed,

$$\ln \sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \beta_1 \ln \sigma_{t-1}^2 + \alpha_1\left(|z_{t-1}| - E|z_{t-1}|\right) + \delta z_{t-1},$$

$$\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \delta,\ \xi,\ \nu).$$

In both models $\delta$ is the asymmetry parameter, and we keep an asymmetric model only if $\hat\delta$ is significant and the information criteria agree. Note that rugarch labels the EGARCH terms differently, its alpha1 is $\delta$ (sign) and its gamma1 is $\alpha_1$ (size). We again use QQ plots to assess the fit of both models, as shown in @fig-qqasym below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-qqasym
#| fig-cap: "QQ plots of the standardised residuals against the fitted skewed t distribution for the GJR-GARCH and EGARCH models."
fit_gjr    <- ugarchfit(make_spec("gjrGARCH", "sstd"), data = returns)
fit_egarch <- ugarchfit(make_spec("eGARCH",   "sstd"), data = returns)

round(fit_gjr@fit$robust.matcoef, 4)
round(fit_egarch@fit$robust.matcoef, 4)

# Standardised residuals and theoretical skewed t quantiles for each model
z_gjr <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_gjr, standardize = TRUE))
q_gjr <- qdist("sstd", p = ppoints(length(z_gjr)), mu = 0, sigma = 1,
               skew = coef(fit_gjr)["skew"], shape = coef(fit_gjr)["shape"])

z_egarch <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_egarch, standardize = TRUE))
q_egarch <- qdist("sstd", p = ppoints(length(z_egarch)), mu = 0, sigma = 1,
                  skew = coef(fit_egarch)["skew"], shape = coef(fit_egarch)["shape"])

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

qqplot(q_gjr, z_gjr, xlab = "Theoretical skewed t quantiles",
       ylab = "Standardised residuals", main = "GJR-GARCH (skewed t)")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")

qqplot(q_egarch, z_egarch, xlab = "Theoretical skewed t quantiles",
       ylab = "Standardised residuals", main = "EGARCH (skewed t)")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The above QQ plots in @fig-qqasym both closely follow the red line, as both models fit the data well. We compare the AIC and BIC of both models to our current best model in @tbl-asym below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-asym
#| tbl-cap: "Log-likelihood, AIC and BIC for the GARCH, GJR-GARCH and EGARCH models with skewed t errors. AIC and BIC are per observation; the log-likelihood is the total."
ic_asym <- cbind(
  GARCH_sstd  = c(infocriteria(fit_st)[1:2, 1],     LogLik = likelihood(fit_st)),
  GJR_sstd    = c(infocriteria(fit_gjr)[1:2, 1],    LogLik = likelihood(fit_gjr)),
  EGARCH_sstd = c(infocriteria(fit_egarch)[1:2, 1], LogLik = likelihood(fit_egarch))
)
round(ic_asym, 4) |> as.data.frame()
```

@tbl-asym shows that both GJR and EGARCH outperform our GARCH model. EGARCH fits marginally better than GJR, but the difference in log-likelihood (0.72) is negligible. As GJR is easier to interpret than EGARCH, and it outperforms our GARCH model, we will use the GJR model. Our model is now as follows,

$$r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{skew-}t_{\xi,\nu}\ (0,1),$$

$$\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \left(\alpha_1 + \delta\,\mathbb{1}[\varepsilon_{t-1}<0]\right)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1\sigma_{t-1}^2,$$

$$\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \delta,\ \xi,\ \nu).$$

## Final Model

The maximum likelihood estimates for each of the parameters in our fitted model is shown in @tbl-gjr-coef.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gjr-coef
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated parameters of the GJR-GARCH(1,1) model with skewed t errors (robust standard errors)."

fit_final <- fit_gjr

round(fit_final@fit$robust.matcoef, 4) |> as.data.frame()
```

By subbing in our estimates from @tbl-gjr-coef above into our model, we get,

$$\hat\theta = (\hat\mu = 0.0186,\ \hat\alpha_0 = 0.0023,\ \hat\alpha_1 = 0.0421,\ \hat\beta_1 = 0.9731,\ \hat\delta = -0.0374,\ \hat\xi = 1.1786,\ \hat\nu = 14.6627),$$

$$\therefore\ r_t = 0.0186 + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{skew-}t_{\xi=1.1786,\ \nu=14.6627}\ (0,1),$$

$$\therefore\ \sigma_t^2 = 0.0023 + \left(0.0421 - 0.0374\,\mathbb{1}[\varepsilon_{t-1}<0]\right)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + 0.9731\,\sigma_{t-1}^2.$$

The errors (or innovations) are modelled as skewed Student t with $\hat\xi = 1.18$ and $\hat\nu = 14.7$. Since $\hat\xi > 1$, large positive standardised shocks (rand depreciation) are more frequent than large negative ones, and $\hat\nu = 14.7$ indicates tails that are heavier than a normal distribution. To check whether the skew is significant, we test $\xi = 1$ (a symmetric distribution) using $t = (\hat\xi - 1)/SE$.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-skew-test
#| tbl-cap: "Test of the skew parameter against 1 (a symmetric distribution)."
cf <- fit_final@fit$robust.matcoef
data.frame(Estimate    = round(cf["skew", 1], 4),
           Std_Error   = round(cf["skew", 2], 4),
           t_statistic = round((cf["skew", 1] - 1) / cf["skew", 2], 2))
```

The t statistic in @tbl-skew-test is about 5.2, so the skew is significant and a symmetric Student t would not be adequate.

## Residual Diagnostics

Now that we have our model, we check the standardised residuals and the squared standardised residuals for any remaining dependence or ARCH effects. @fig-resid shows the residuals and their ACFs, and @tbl-diag shows the tests below. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-resid
#| fig-cap: "Standardised residuals of the GJR-GARCH model over time, and the ACFs of the standardised, squared and absolute standardised residuals."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
z <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_final, standardize = TRUE))

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(z, pch = 16, cex = 0.3, xlab = "Time", ylab = "Standardised residual",
     main = "Standardised residuals")
acf(z,      main = "ACF of standardised residuals")
acf(z^2,    main = "ACF of squared standardised residuals")
acf(abs(z), main = "ACF of absolute standardised residuals")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diag
#| tbl-cap: "Diagnostic tests on the standardised residuals of the GJR-GARCH model (p-values; large values are the outcome we want)."
diag_tab <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Ljung-Box on z (mean equation)",
           "Ljung-Box on z^2 (variance equation)",
           "Ljung-Box on |z|",
           "ARCH LM test on z"),
  p_value = c(Box.test(z,      lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value,
              Box.test(z^2,    lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value,
              Box.test(abs(z), lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value,
              ArchTest(z, lags = 10)$p.value)
)
transform(diag_tab, p_value = round(p_value, 3))
```

In @fig-resid, the standardised residuals plot shows no obvious pattern or volatility clustering. The ACF of standardised residuals has only a few isolated lags just outside the bounds, and the Ljung-Box test finds no overall autocorrelation, so there is no evidence of any remaining linear dependence. The ACFs of squared and absolute standardised residuals show significant lags at the first few lags (lags 1 and 2 for both, plus lag 3 for the absolute residuals and lag 10 for the squared residuals), so there may be some remaining weak short-lag dependence in volatility. @tbl-diag shows that the mean equation is adequate (Ljung-Box on $\hat z_t$, $p = 0.65$), but the Ljung-Box tests on $\hat z_t^2$ and $|\hat z_t|$ and the ARCH LM test are significant ($p \le 0.009$). Together with the ACFs, this indicates weak, short-lag volatility dependence that the GJR-GARCH(1,1) does not capture, which we will treat as a limitation.

## Persistence 

We are interested in how long the effect of a shock persists. For the standard GARCH(1,1) model, $\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1\sigma_{t-1}^2$, the persistence is how slowly a volatility shock fades (close to 1 means very slowly), and is defined as,

$$\rho = \alpha_1 + \beta_1.$$

If $\rho < 1$, the unconditional variance is the long-run average variance that volatility reverts to, and is calculated as,

$$\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_t) = E(\sigma_t^2) = \frac{\alpha_0}{1-\rho}.$$

The long-run daily volatility is the square root of the unconditional variance, and is the typical size of a daily move in percent. The half-life of a volatility shock is the number of days for its effect to halve, and is approximately,

$$h_{1/2} = \frac{\log(0.5)}{\log(\rho)}, \qquad 0 < \rho < 1.$$

Our model differs in its variance equation, which has the extra asymmetry term,

$$\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \left(\alpha_1 + \delta\,\mathbb{1}[\varepsilon_{t-1}<0]\right)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1\sigma_{t-1}^2.$$

Negative shocks carry the extra effect $\delta$, so they enter the persistence as well. With about half of the shocks negative, the persistence becomes

$$\rho = \alpha_1 + \frac{\delta}{2} + \beta_1.$$

We use the same expressions for the unconditional variance and half-life with this $\rho$.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-persistence
#| tbl-cap: "Persistence, half-life, long-run variance and long-run volatility of the final model."
data.frame(
  Measure = c("Persistence", "Half-life (trading days)", "Long-run variance", "Long-run volatility (% per day)"),
  Value   = round(c(persistence(fit_final),
                    log(0.5) / log(persistence(fit_final)),
                    uncvariance(fit_final),
                    sqrt(uncvariance(fit_final))), 4)
)
```

We take the estimates in @tbl-persistence from rugarch, which computes the share of negative shocks from the fitted skewed t distribution, giving $\hat\rho = 0.9956$, a long-run variance of $0.518$ (a volatility of $0.72\%$ per day) and a half-life of about $158$ trading days. Persistence this close to 1 means shocks to volatility fade very slowly, with the effect of a shock taking about seven to eight months to halve, so periods of high or low volatility last a long time. The estimated reaction to a positive shock is $\hat\alpha_1 = 0.042$ and the memory of past volatility is $\hat\beta_1 = 0.973$, while $\hat\delta = -0.037$ (significant) cuts the effect of a negative shock to $\hat\alpha_1 + \hat\delta = 0.005$, so volatility rises mostly after positive returns, when the rand weakens.

The mean $\hat\mu = 0.0186$ is the average daily return, about 0.02% a day. This is tiny compared with the typical daily move of 0.7% to 1%, so the rand barely drifts on average and the day-to-day changes are mostly noise, as for a random walk. The constant $\hat\alpha_0 = 0.0023$ is the fixed amount added to the variance each day, regardless of the previous shock. It is small on its own, but the long-run variance divides it by $1 - \rho = 0.0044$, which gives $0.0023 / 0.0044 \approx 0.52$. This also explains why the long-run level is so uncertain, as when $\rho$ is close to 1, a small change in the estimates makes a large change in that division.

## Volatility Forecast

Having fitted the model, we look at its estimated conditional volatility over time and at its 20-day volatility forecast, shown in @fig-vol below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-vol
#| fig-cap: "Estimated daily conditional volatility of USD/ZAR (left) and the 20-day volatility forecast (right) from the GJR-GARCH(1,1) model with skewed t errors. The dashed line is the long-run volatility."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
rdates <- data_clean$date[-1]      # dates that match `returns`
long_run <- sqrt(uncvariance(fit_final))

fc <- ugarchforecast(fit_final, n.ahead = 20)
sig_f <- as.numeric(sigma(fc))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(rdates, as.numeric(sigma(fit_final)), type = "l", xlab = "",
     ylab = "conditional sd (%)", main = "Estimated daily volatility")
abline(h = long_run, col = "red", lty = 2)

plot(1:20, sig_f, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "days ahead",
     ylab = "forecast volatility (% per day)", main = "20-day forecast",
     ylim = range(sig_f, long_run))
abline(h = long_run, col = "red", lty = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The left panel of @fig-vol shows that the estimated volatility of the rand moves in clear waves. It peaks in 2016 and 2018, at about 1.5% a day, and most sharply in early 2020 at about 1.75% (this is possibly related to COVID-19 which started in 2020), and then falls back each time. Volatility is above the model’s long-run level of 0.72% for most of the sample, and falls to its lowest point, about 0.5% a day, by the end of 2025.

Because volatility is currently low, the 20-day forecast in the right panel rises from 0.48% to 0.50% a day, heading towards the long-run level. It rises only slowly, since persistence is close to 1, so only a small part of the gap closes in 20 days. The forecast says nothing about the direction of the rand, only about how large daily moves are likely to be.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-long-run
#| tbl-cap: "Sample standard deviation of the returns, average fitted volatility and the model's long-run volatility (% per day)."
data.frame(
  Measure = c("Sample standard deviation of returns",
              "Average fitted volatility",
              "Model's long-run volatility"),
  Value   = round(c(sd(returns),
                    mean(as.numeric(sigma(fit_final))),
                    sqrt(uncvariance(fit_final))), 2)
)
```

@tbl-long-run shows that the model’s implied long-run volatility is 0.72% per day, but the sample standard deviation of the returns is 0.96% and the average fitted volatility is 0.94%, so the model's long-run level is probably underestimated, because it depends on $\hat\alpha_0$ (not significant) and on persistence very close to one.

## Model Predictions and Actual Data Comparison

We now compare our model, including the conditional variance for our prediction intervals, with our actual data, shown in @fig-price-band below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-price-band
#| fig-cap: "Actual USD/ZAR price, one-day-ahead predicted price and the 95% prediction band from the GJR-GARCH model: full sample (top) and the most recent year (bottom)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
mu_hat <- coef(fit_final)["mu"]
s      <- as.numeric(sigma(fit_final))
p_prev <- data_clean$exchange_rate[-nrow(data_clean)]
p_act  <- data_clean$exchange_rate[-1]

band <- tibble(date = rdates, price = p_act, r = returns,
               pred = p_prev * exp(mu_hat / 100),
               lo   = p_prev * exp((mu_hat - 2 * s) / 100),
               hi   = p_prev * exp((mu_hat + 2 * s) / 100),
               r_lo = mu_hat - 2 * s, r_hi = mu_hat + 2 * s)

band_both <- bind_rows(
  band |> mutate(panel = "Full sample"),
  band |> filter(date >= as.Date("2025-01-01")) |> mutate(panel = "Most recent year (2025)")
) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = c("Full sample", "Most recent year (2025)")),
         pred  = ifelse(panel == "Full sample", NA_real_, pred))

ggplot(band_both, aes(date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = "95% prediction band"), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred, colour = "Predicted price"), linetype = "dashed",
            linewidth = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = price, colour = "Actual price"), linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("95% prediction band" = "red")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Actual price" = "black", "Predicted price" = "blue")) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "", y = "rand per dollar", fill = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The predicted price is essentially yesterday’s price, as expected for an exchange rate whose returns are uncorrelated, so the model’s contribution is the width of the prediction band. Over the full sample the band is widest around early 2020, and in 2025 it widens in April and then narrows steadily as the year becomes calmer.

## Fitted Volatility

@fig-fitted-band plots the daily returns against plus and minus two fitted conditional standard deviations from our model (red), and against the band that a constant-variance model would give (blue, plus and minus two sample standard deviations).

```{r}
#| label: fig-fitted-band
#| fig-cap: "Daily log returns with the 95% prediction band from the GJR-GARCH model and the constant-variance band: full sample (top) and the most recent year 2025 (bottom)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
m        <- mean(returns)
sd_const <- sd(returns)

ggplot(band_both, aes(date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = r, colour = "Daily return"), linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = m + 2 * sd_const, colour = "Constant-variance band"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = m - 2 * sd_const, colour = "Constant-variance band"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = r_hi, colour = "GJR-GARCH band"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = r_lo, colour = "GJR-GARCH band"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Daily return" = "grey50",
                                 "GJR-GARCH band" = "red",
                                 "Constant-variance band" = "blue")) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "", y = "daily log return (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The constant-variance band is the same width throughout, so it is too narrow in turbulent periods (such as 2016 and early 2020, when many returns fall outside it) and too wide in calm ones, whereas the GARCH band widens and narrows with the volatility, reaching about ±3.5% in early 2020 and narrowing to about ±1% by the end of the sample.

## Price Forecast

Finally, we use the model to forecast the exchange rate 20 trading days beyond the end of the data. @fig-price-forecast shows the last three months of 2025 and the forecast price with its 95% prediction band. As the daily returns are uncorrelated, the variances add up over the horizon, so the band at day $h$ uses the cumulative variance $\sum_{k=1}^{h} \hat\sigma_{T+k}^2$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-price-forecast
#| fig-cap: "Actual USD/ZAR price for the last three months of 2025, and the 20-day-ahead price forecast with its 95% prediction band from the GJR-GARCH model."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
p_last <- tail(data_clean$exchange_rate, 1)
d_last <- tail(data_clean$date, 1)
h      <- 1:20
cum_sd <- sqrt(cumsum(sig_f^2))   # sd of the cumulative return over h days

fdates <- seq(d_last + 1, by = "day", length.out = 40)
fdates <- fdates[as.integer(format(fdates, "%u")) <= 5][1:20]   # weekdays only

fc_tab <- tibble(date = fdates,
                 pred = p_last * exp(mu_hat * h / 100),
                 lo   = p_last * exp((mu_hat * h - 2 * cum_sd) / 100),
                 hi   = p_last * exp((mu_hat * h + 2 * cum_sd) / 100))

recent <- band |> filter(date >= as.Date("2025-10-01"))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = recent, aes(date, price, colour = "Actual price")) +
  geom_ribbon(data = fc_tab, aes(date, ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = "95% prediction band"), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = fc_tab, aes(date, pred, colour = "Forecast price"), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("95% prediction band" = "red")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Actual price" = "black", "Forecast price" = "blue")) +
  labs(x = "", y = "rand per dollar", fill = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The forecast price is almost flat at about R16.6 per dollar, which is essentially the last observed price. It rises very slightly because the estimated mean return is a small positive drift ($\hat\mu = 0.0186\%$ a day), which adds up to only about 0.4% over 20 days, much smaller than the width of the band. The model's information is in the band, which starts at about R16.4 to R16.7 on day 1 and widens to about R15.9 to R17.4 by day 20. It widens because uncertainty accumulates over the days, which makes the band a cone rather than parallel lines. The forecast says nothing about the direction of the rand, only how far it could plausibly move.

The volatility forecast and prediction bands are useful for risk management, for example setting risk limits and value-at-risk figures that tighten in calm periods and widen in turbulent ones, or deciding how much exposure to the rand to hedge. They have limits, though. They say nothing about the direction of the rand, since the point forecast is essentially the last price. The residual tests showed some remaining volatility dependence the model misses. The long-run level is poorly estimated, and the forecasts rely on the 2015 to 2025 data, so they cannot anticipate a sudden event or structural break such as the April 2025 spike.

## Reflection

The hardest part was keeping apart ideas that sound similar. I first thought that skewed t errors and the GJR-GARCH or EGARCH models did the same job, since both are about asymmetry, but they are not the same thing. The skewed t describes the shape of the error distribution $z_t$ (whether large positive and negative standardised shocks are equally likely), while GJR and EGARCH change how the variance reacts to the sign of the previous shock. Once I separated them I could fit and compare both properly. I also found that packages and textbooks use different parameterisations. In `rugarch`, the EGARCH `alpha1` is the sign term and `gamma1` the size term, which is the reverse of my notes, so I had to check the formulas against the output rather than trust the names.

Residual diagnostics took me a long time. I did not expect the model to still show dependence after a good QQ plot and good information criteria. I had to work out that the Ljung-Box test on $\hat z_t$ checks the mean equation and the test on $\hat z_t^2$ checks the variance equation, which showed my mean equation was fine while a little volatility dependence remained. I tried GJR(2,1) and GJR(1,2) to remove it, and neither did, so I report it as a limitation rather than hide it. I also had to learn that persistence for the GJR model is not simply $\alpha_1 + \beta_1$, and that the long-run variance can be badly estimated when persistence is close to one, as my 0.72% a day is well below the sample standard deviation of 0.96%.

Through this project I learned that choosing a model is a sequence of small decisions, each backed by evidence. For example, a constant mean from the Ljung-Box test and ARMA comparison, skewed t errors from QQ plots and AIC/BIC, and GJR over EGARCH because the fit was almost the same and GJR is easier to interpret. I also learned how to read the output, such as testing the skew with $(\hat\xi - 1)/SE$ rather than the package's p-value, which tests against zero. Plotting the model against the data taught me the most about what GARCH does. The point forecast of an exchange rate is just yesterday's price, and the value of the model is in the width of the band, which was widest in early 2020 and in the April 2025 spike. A constant-variance band has the same overall coverage, but it misses far more of the turbulent days.

If I did this again, I would first try other variance structures to deal with the leftover dependence. I would refit the model before and after 2020 to check for a structural break, and evaluate the forecasts out of sample instead of only fitting in sample. I planned to write my own GARCH(1,1) log-likelihood and compare it to `rugarch`, but dropped it because of time, so my estimates rely on the package. I would also use a news impact curve to show the asymmetry visually, and I would investigate the six extreme returns I removed, to see whether they are data errors or real market events, rather than simply excluding them.

The most interesting result for me was that a model with an almost-zero mean and strongly persistent volatility describes the rand well, which matches what I'd expect of an exchange rate that moves like a random walk with changing risk.
